easy.text: Admiral Zheng He led a series of massive maritime expeditions, known as the 'treasure voyages,' on behalf of which Chinese dynasty?

options.feedback: Correct -- Zheng He's fleets sailed under the authority of the Ming dynasty, starting in the early 15th century.
The Qing dynasty, founded by Manchu rulers, came centuries after Zheng He's voyages.
The Tang dynasty was an earlier golden age, centuries before Zheng He's era.
The Han dynasty ruled over a thousand years before Zheng He's voyages.

medium.text: Zheng He's fleets, sailing between 1405 and 1433, reached as far as which region, well beyond Southeast Asia and India?

options.feedback: Correct -- Zheng He's ships reached East African ports, an extraordinary distance for the time.
There is no credible evidence Zheng He's fleets reached the Americas.
Zheng He's voyages never reached Western Europe -- their furthest known extent was East Africa.
Zheng He's fleets are not documented as having reached Australia.

hard.text: What brought the treasure voyages to an end in the mid-15th century, after which China turned away from large-scale state-sponsored maritime expansion?

options.text: A shift in Ming court politics toward isolationism and fiscal retrenchment
options.feedback: Correct -- after the Yongle Emperor's death, court factions favoring internal stability and reduced spending gained influence and ended the costly expeditions.

options.text: A catastrophic naval defeat by a European power
options.feedback: No European power defeated Zheng He's fleets -- the end of the voyages was a domestic political and fiscal decision.

options.text: The completion of the Great Wall
options.feedback: The Great Wall's construction is unrelated to the decision to end the treasure voyages.

options.text: A famine that wiped out China's shipbuilding regions
options.feedback: There's no basis for this -- the voyages ended due to shifting court priorities, not a famine destroying shipbuilding capacity.

easy.easy: This dynasty ruled China from the 14th to the mid-17th century, right before the Manchu-led Qing dynasty took over.
easy.medium: This dynasty also built the Forbidden City and sent these voyages under Emperor Yongle.
easy.hard: Think of the Chinese dynasty that ruled just before the Manchu-led dynasty took over.

medium.easy: The fleets reached ports near modern-day Kenya and Somalia, on the continent that lies just across the Indian Ocean from India.
medium.medium: Think of a continent bordering the Indian Ocean, west of India.
medium.hard: The fleets sailed far past Southeast Asia and India.

hard.easy: After Yongle died, the Ming court's priorities turned inward, favoring internal stability and lower spending over continued costly expeditions.
hard.medium: The change was political and financial, not the result of losing a battle.
hard.hard: After a powerful emperor died, more conservative officials gained influence at court.

easy.text: In which city is the Forbidden City, the former imperial palace complex, located?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Forbidden City sits at the heart of Beijing, China's capital.

Xi'an is famous for the Terracotta Army, not the Forbidden City.

The Qing dynasty later occupied the Forbidden City, but did not build it.
The Tang dynasty ruled centuries before the Forbidden City was built.
The Song dynasty predates the Forbidden City's construction by centuries.

hard.text: Besides the Ming, which other dynasty continued to use the Forbidden City as its seat of imperial power until the fall of China's monarchy in the early 20th century?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Manchu-led Qing dynasty ruled from the Forbidden City until China's monarchy ended in 1912.
The Yuan dynasty predates the Forbidden City's construction -- it ruled before the Ming.
The Republic that followed the monarchy's fall did not rule from the Forbidden City as an imperial seat.
The Song dynasty ruled long before the Forbidden City existed.

easy.easy: This city is China's capital today.
easy.medium: This city is in northern China and has been China's capital for centuries.

medium.medium: This dynasty ruled before the Manchu conquest of China.
medium.hard: This dynasty's Yongle Emperor ordered the palace's construction in the early 15th century.

hard.medium: This dynasty was established by Manchu rulers from the northeast.
hard.hard: This dynasty's rule lasted until 1912, when China became a republic.

topic: The Sengoku period and the rise of the samurai

easy.text: The Sengoku ('Warring States') period was an era of near-constant civil war among rival warlords in which country?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Sengoku period was a roughly century-long era of civil war among Japan's feudal lords.
China had its own separate periods of internal conflict, but the Sengoku period specifically refers to Japan.
Korea is distinct from Japan, where the Sengoku period took place.
Vietnam is unrelated to the Sengoku period, which was a Japanese era.

medium.text: The Sengoku period's regional warlords, who commanded samurai armies while battling for control of Japan, were known by what title?

options.feedback: Correct -- daimyo were the powerful feudal lords who ruled territories and led samurai armies during the Sengoku period.
A shogun was the singular overall military ruler over all of Japan, a title distinct from the many competing regional lords.
Samurai were the warrior class the daimyo commanded, not the title for the lords themselves.
Japan's emperor held largely symbolic authority during this era, not the title for the feuding regional warlords.

hard.text: Select all individuals traditionally credited as the 'three great unifiers' who brought Japan's Sengoku period to an end. (Select all that apply)

options.feedback: Correct -- Nobunaga began the process of reunifying Japan before his death.
Correct -- Hideyoshi continued Nobunaga's work and further consolidated power across Japan.
Correct -- Ieyasu completed the unification and founded the shogunate that ruled Japan for over two centuries.
Minamoto Yoritomo founded an earlier shogunate in the 12th century, centuries before the Sengoku period's unifiers.
Miyamoto Musashi was a famed swordsman and duelist, not one of the political unifiers of Japan.

easy.easy: This country's feudal era of civil war eventually ended with the Tokugawa shogunate.
easy.medium: This country's warrior class is famously known as the samurai.

topic: China's invention of movable type printing

easy.text: Long before Gutenberg's press appeared in Europe, which country's inventor developed movable type printing technology?

options.feedback: Correct -- movable type printing was developed in China centuries before Gutenberg's press.
Japan adopted printing technologies but movable type's origin is credited to China.
India is not credited with this invention -- it originated in China.
Ancient Egypt is known for early writing systems, but not for inventing movable type printing.

medium.text: Who is credited with inventing movable type printing in 11th-century China, using individual characters made of fired clay?

options.feedback: Correct -- Bi Sheng developed ceramic movable type printing during the Song dynasty.
Cai Lun is credited with an earlier invention, papermaking, not movable type printing.
Confucius was an ancient philosopher who lived many centuries before movable type was invented.
Zhang Heng was a scientist known for inventing an early seismoscope, not movable type printing.

hard.text: Despite predating Gutenberg's press by about four centuries, why did movable type not fully replace woodblock printing in China at the time?

options.text: Because the thousands of unique Chinese characters made a movable type system less efficient than for alphabetic languages
options.feedback: Correct -- managing thousands of individual character blocks offered less of an efficiency advantage than it did for languages using a small alphabet.

options.text: Because the Chinese government banned printing technology
options.feedback: There was no such government ban -- the limitation was practical efficiency given the writing system.

options.text: Because paper had not yet been invented in China
options.feedback: Paper had already been invented in China centuries earlier -- this wasn't the limiting factor.

options.text: Because movable type was invented after printing had already died out in China
options.feedback: Printing, especially woodblock printing, continued to thrive in China alongside and after movable type's invention.

easy.easy: This is the same country famous for inventing paper centuries earlier.
easy.medium: This East Asian country's Song dynasty produced this innovation.
easy.hard: This country's invention predates Gutenberg's European press by roughly four centuries.

medium.easy: This person's invention used individual characters made of a fired, clay-like material.
medium.medium: This person is distinct from the earlier inventor credited with papermaking.
medium.hard: This person worked during the Song dynasty, centuries before Gutenberg, using ceramic character blocks.

hard.medium: The issue was practical efficiency, not a government ban or a lack of paper.
hard.hard: Think about how many different characters the Chinese writing system uses compared to an alphabet.

topic: Vasco da Gama's voyage to India

easy.text: Vasco da Gama, sailing for Portugal, became the first European to reach India by sea by sailing around which African landmark?

options.feedback: Correct -- da Gama's fleet rounded the Cape of Good Hope at Africa's southern tip on the way to India.

The Strait of Gibraltar connects the Mediterranean and Atlantic, but it wasn't the key landmark on da Gama's route to India.
The Nile Delta is in northern Egypt, not the southern African landmark da Gama's route rounded.

medium.text: What was the primary economic motivation driving Portugal's search for a sea route to India, achieved by da Gama in 1498?

options.text: Gaining direct access to the valuable spice trade, bypassing Middle Eastern middlemen
options.feedback: Correct -- a direct sea route let Portugal trade for spices without relying on Middle Eastern and Italian intermediaries.

options.text: Searching for gold deposits in a newly discovered continent
options.feedback: That motivation is more associated with Spain's voyages to the Americas, not da Gama's route to India.

options.text: Establishing a colony for large-scale European settlement
options.feedback: Da Gama's voyage was primarily driven by trade access, not settlement colonization.

options.text: Spreading printing press technology to Asia
options.feedback: Printing technology was not the motivation behind da Gama's voyage -- trade in valuable goods was.

hard.text: Da Gama's fleet, arriving in India in 1498, made its first landing at which port city on India's southwestern coast?

options.feedback: Correct -- da Gama landed at Calicut, known today as Kozhikode, in 1498.
Mumbai (then Bombay) became prominent under later colonial rule, not as da Gama's first landing point.
Goa became a major Portuguese colony, but only years after da Gama's initial 1498 landing at Calicut.

easy.text: Ferdinand Magellan's expedition, sailing for Spain, achieved what historic first, even though Magellan himself died partway through?

options.text: Completing the first circumnavigation of the globe

Magellan's route did not go around the Cape of Good Hope -- and his death occurred in the Philippines.

options.feedback: Correct -- Elcano brought the sole surviving ship, the Victoria, back to Spain in 1522, completing the circumnavigation.

easy.text: What term describes the widespread transfer of plants, animals, diseases, and people between the Americas and the rest of the world following Columbus's voyages?

options.text: Old World diseases, like smallpox, to which native populations had no immunity

options.text: Competition from newly introduced Old World crops

Loss of gold was an economic consequence for some empires, but not the exchange's most devastating human cost.

topic: The Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire

topic: Peter the Great and the modernization of Russia

medium.text: Peter the Great founded which city, built from scratch on the Baltic coast, to serve as Russia's new capital and 'window to the West'?

options.feedback: Correct -- Peter built St. Petersburg on the Baltic coast as Russia's new capital, linking it more closely to Western Europe.
Moscow was Russia's older, existing capital -- Peter built a brand-new city rather than relying on it.
Kiev is an older city with a separate historical significance, not the new capital Peter founded.
Novgorod is an ancient Russian city, not the new capital Peter the Great established.

hard.text: Peter the Great's long war against Sweden, which established Russia as a major Baltic power, is known as what?

options.feedback: Correct -- this early 18th-century war against Sweden secured Russia's dominance over the Baltic region.
The Crimean War occurred in the mid-19th century, over a century after Peter's reign.
The Livonian War was an earlier 16th-century conflict, fought under a different ruler.
The Seven Years' War was a mid-18th-century global conflict, distinct from Peter's war against Sweden.

easy.medium: This tsar is known for traveling incognito through Western Europe to learn shipbuilding and other skills.
easy.hard: This ruler is distinct from a later Russian empress with a similar epithet.

hard.medium: This long war was fought against a Scandinavian rival power.

easy.text: Catherine the Great, one of Russia's most powerful rulers, reigned as empress during which century?

options.feedback: Correct -- Catherine the Great reigned from 1762 to 1796, in the 18th century.
The 16th century was too early -- Catherine's reign fell in the 18th century.
The 19th century was too late -- Catherine's reign ended before it began.
The 14th century is centuries too early for Catherine the Great's reign.

medium.text: How did Catherine the Great come to power as empress of Russia?

options.text: Through a coup that deposed her husband, Emperor Peter III
options.feedback: Correct -- Catherine seized power in a palace coup that ended her husband's short, unpopular reign.

options.text: She inherited the throne directly from her father
options.feedback: Catherine was not born into the Russian royal family and did not inherit the throne from a father -- she rose through a coup against her husband.

options.text: She was elected by the Russian nobility in an open vote
options.feedback: Russia had no such electoral system for choosing its ruler -- Catherine gained power through a palace coup.

options.text: She won the throne through a war of succession against a rival branch of the family
options.feedback: Catherine's rise involved a palace coup against her own husband, not a broader war of succession.

hard.text: Catherine the Great's reign significantly expanded Russian territory southward, gaining access to which body of water through wars against the Ottoman Empire?

options.feedback: Correct -- Catherine's wars against the Ottomans secured Russian access to warm-water ports on the Black Sea, including Crimea.
Baltic access was primarily secured earlier, under Peter the Great, not through Catherine's Ottoman wars.
The Caspian Sea was not the primary body of water gained through Catherine's Ottoman wars -- that was the Black Sea.
Russia did not annex Mediterranean coastline through these wars -- the key gain was Black Sea access.

easy.easy: This century falls between the Renaissance era and the 19th century's industrial age.
easy.medium: This century also saw the American and French Revolutions.
easy.hard: This is the century immediately following Peter the Great's own reign in Russia.

medium.medium: Her rise involved removing her own spouse from power.
medium.hard: Think about how she gained the throne -- not peacefully by simple inheritance.

hard.medium: This is a different sea from the one Peter the Great had already secured access to.
hard.hard: This body of water lies to Russia's south, bordered partly by the Ottoman Empire's former territory.

topic: The Zulu Kingdom and Shaka Zulu

easy.text: Shaka is the founding king most associated with building which powerful African kingdom in the early 19th century?

options.feedback: Correct -- Shaka founded and built up the Zulu Kingdom into a dominant regional power in southern Africa.
The Ashanti Empire was located in West Africa, a separate kingdom from Shaka's Zulu Kingdom.
The Kingdom of Kongo was in central Africa, a different region and era from Shaka's Zulu Kingdom.
The Ethiopian Empire is a much older, separate polity in a different region of Africa.

medium.text: Shaka Zulu is credited with major military innovations, including a new short stabbing spear and what famous tactical battle formation?

options.feedback: Correct -- this formation split forces into a 'chest' and two 'horns' to encircle and overwhelm opposing armies.
The phalanx was an ancient Greek formation, unrelated to Shaka's Zulu military innovations.
The testudo formation was used by ancient Roman legions, not Shaka's Zulu forces.
Trench warfare became prominent in World War I, nearly a century after Shaka's era.

hard.text: Shaka's rise and the Zulu Kingdom's expansion in the early 19th century contributed to a period of widespread warfare, displacement, and state formation across southern Africa known by what term?

options.feedback: Correct -- the Mfecane describes the era of upheaval, migration, and state formation linked to the Zulu Kingdom's rise.
The Scramble for Africa refers to later 19th-century European colonization, a different phenomenon from the Mfecane.
The Boer Wars were later conflicts against British and Dutch settlers, distinct from the Mfecane upheaval.
Apartheid was a 20th-century system of racial segregation, an entirely different era and topic.
